student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. Mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools.
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in informatics fluency; assume no prior training in health data standards. Learners engage best with REAL record examples — actual note text, lab values with their metadata, imaging headers — not abstract definitions. Plain language, terms defined on first use, short daily sessions.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This module teaches HEALTHCARE DATA as the foundation for AI in healthcare, and it is structured EXACTLY as four learning objectives, in this fixed order: (1) map the major healthcare data sources; (2) distinguish structured from unstructured data; (3) recognize data quality and interoperability issues; (4) apply ethical and governance frameworks. The module's framing line is: AI is only as good as the data behind it — knowing the data is knowing what AI can and cannot do. AI itself appears only as brief context (data is what any downstream tool consumes; data quality bounds tool reliability), never as a session's subject. Every named fact, definition, standard, and example MUST come from the provided source excerpts; never invent an example, statistic, or citation. Where the sources do not cover a named subtopic (for example omics data, patient-generated data, administrative claims data, or a specific consent regulation), either describe it generically in one sentence or omit it — NEVER invent specifics for it. When citing a named source or standard, its URL from the excerpts appears on the slide. NAMING RULE: refer to the provided materials as 'the source' or by the document's own name (the FHIR specification, the OHDSI handbook, the record-definitions article, the DICOM paper, the documentation-fundamentals article); NEVER write 'textbook', 'the chapter', or 'students'.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Visual-first, punchy slides modeled on the client's own decks — NEVER walls of bullets. Most slides carry ONE idea in at most 30 words of body text: a big statement, a short quoted dialogue, a figure with a two-line explanation, or a compact table. Directly under each frame title, put a one-line italic message stating the slide's takeaway. When a figure from the source excerpts fits the slide, the figure DOMINATES the slide with at most two short lines of text beside or below it. The lecture script carries the depth; the slides carry the punch. Open every session with a real hook from the sources; close every session with a knowledge check.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess data literacy per objective: naming where a given piece of clinical data lives, telling structured from unstructured data and why it matters for AI, spotting a quality or interoperability problem in a record fragment, and identifying the governance question a data reuse raises. No exams, no coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: By the end of this module, learners will be able to: (1) map the major healthcare data sources — what each contains and how it is stored; (2) distinguish structured from unstructured data — lab values versus free-text notes, and why the proportion matters for AI development; (3) recognize data quality and interoperability issues — missingness, coding inconsistency, FHIR, OMOP, and why hospitals struggle to share data; (4) apply ethical and governance frameworks — consent, de-identification, secondary use, and data ownership in research and AI training.
course_structure.total_number_of_weeks: 1 module of EXACTLY 4 sessions — one session per learning objective, equal length
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline: The module has EXACTLY FOUR sessions, one per learning objective, in this fixed order — do not merge, split, add, or reorder. Each session teaches ONLY its objective and assumes the earlier sessions were completed: never re-teach another session's content (at most one referring sentence). Session 1 — Map the major healthcare data sources: what the medical record is (legal medical record, designated record set, EHR as a datastore); one patient, many systems — where clinical data lives and how each source stores it (EHR, laboratory, pharmacy, imaging archive/PACS), taught through real record artifacts from the sources; other source types the sources do not cover (omics, patient-generated, administrative) named only generically. EXCLUDE: coded-versus-narrative comparisons (Session 2), exchange standards and FHIR/OMOP mechanics (Session 3), governance (Session 4). Session 2 — Distinguish structured from unstructured data: coded, countable entries (LOINC laboratory codes, RxNorm normalized drug names and RXCUIs, DICOM enumerated values and coded entries, OMOP standard concepts) versus free-text clinical notes (what good documentation carries that codes cannot); why the structured/unstructured proportion matters for any downstream tool. EXCLUDE: interoperability and exchange (Session 3), open science, FAIR, data-model design principles, ETL, and governance (Session 4). Session 3 — Recognize data quality and interoperability issues: the same clinical fact represented differently in two systems; missingness and coding inconsistency taught through record fragments; how exchange standards address it — FHIR resources and profiles, the OMOP common data model and standardized vocabularies as the research shape, DICOM as the imaging interchange standard; why hospitals still struggle to share data. ETL/mapping appears in AT MOST ONE slide (mapping source codes to standard concepts is where errors appear). EXCLUDE: ETL unit testing, ETL maintenance triggers, vocabulary-release management, open science, and anything already taught in Sessions 1-2. Session 4 — Apply ethical and governance frameworks: only what the sources support on consent, de-identification, secondary use, and data ownership — the record as a legal document and the duty of documentation; correcting the record transparently; what may be released versus protected (designated record set decisions); data protection by design in research data models (limiting identifying details); permission, licensing, and provenance before reuse. ZERO slides about open science, FAIR, the OHDSI community, reproducibility, or 'open data / open source / open discourse' — these are NOT governance content for this audience and must not appear at all. Governance here means: which record is official and releasable, the duty to document and to correct transparently, objective wording because patients and courts read the chart, limiting identifiers in research data, and asking who permitted a reuse. The session MUST END with three slides in this order: one discussion-cases slide (3-4 numbered one-line cases, each with a one-line setup), one knowledge-check slide (exactly 3 questions, no answers), one answers slide. EXCLUDE: re-teaching record definitions, structured-versus-unstructured, or interoperability (Sessions 1-3). This session stays shorter rather than inventing regulatory content the sources lack.

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Per-session knowledge checks (3 questions, answers on the following slide). Record Reading — given a real fragment, identify its source system, whether it is structured, what quality issue it shows, or what governance question it raises.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Short applied checks inside each deck; self-paced.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Institution-approved learning platform; accessibility standards; no patient-identifiable information. Named tools, studies, and standards are permitted when drawn from the provided public sources with attribution.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; no teaching assistant assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development; each session is a self-paced ~35-minute module tied to one learning objective. All four sessions must be the SAME length: 18-22 slides each, hard cap 24.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for health-data literacy and responsible use of clinical information systems.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: All named examples, statistics, and cases must be traceable to the provided public sources (attribution on slide); no fabricated content; no patient-identifiable information.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Module must include learning outcomes, the four-session structure (one session per objective), the assessment approach, and a sources page listing every cited source with its URL.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: Revision after client review: the previous version organized content BY SOURCE (one section per standard), which read as disorganized. The client's own lecture materials structure a session as ORDERED LEARNING OBJECTIVES, with the standards woven in where they serve an objective (FHIR and OMOP belong under data quality and interoperability, not as standalone sections). Equal reading time per objective was an explicit client request.

session_structure: Each chapter of this course IS one session and covers exactly ONE of the four learning objectives, in the fixed order given, teaching ONLY that objective's scope as listed in the schedule (obey its EXCLUDE list; never re-teach another session's content). Every session: opens with a slide stating its objective in the client's phrasing plus a one-line takeaway, then a real record moment from the sources; is built AROUND 3-5 worked record examples (at most a third of slides purely conceptual); closes with ONE discussion-cases slide, ONE knowledge-check slide of exactly 3 questions, and ONE answers slide (answers NEVER on the question slide). LENGTH: EXACTLY 18-22 slides, hard cap 24 — count them; all four sessions the same length.
engagement_style: ONE THING PER SLIDE — every slide holds exactly one definition-in-use, one worked record example, one table, or one question; never combine two ideas; body text at most 45 words unless the slide is a table or the answers slide. (1) The first content slide states the session's learning objective and its takeaway line; the next slide is a real record moment from the sources — never an abstract framework. (2) WORKED RECORD EXAMPLES are the backbone — 3-5 per session, each on its OWN slide: show a small real record fragment or value from the sources, ask what a careful reader must know, then walk what the source, structure, standard, or governance rule adds. (3) Session 1 MUST include one 'One patient, many systems' TABLE slide: rows = data types (notes, labs, imaging, medications), columns = where it lives and how it is stored, rendered with the LaTeX colorbox command as short chips — this table belongs ONLY in Session 1. (4) Session 2 MUST include one slide contrasting THE SAME clinical fact as a coded entry versus as note text, built from source material. (5) Session 3 MUST include one worked interoperability example: the same data element represented differently in two systems, and what the exchange standard does about it. (6) Session 4 contains NO open-science / FAIR / OHDSI-community / reproducibility slides (zero) and MUST end with discussion cases, a 3-question knowledge check, and an answers slide; Session 4 MUST include one PROVENANCE-AND-PERMISSION questions slide: the questions a careful reader asks about origin, purpose, transformation, and permission to reuse, phrased as questions drawn from the sources. (7) Each session includes exactly ONE discussion-cases slide: 3-4 numbered one-line judgment scenarios with no clean answer, each with a one-line setup context, tied to that session's objective. (8) TONE: slide titles are active and curiosity-driven, never bureaucratic. (9) REGISTER: the audience is practicing clinicians and healthcare staff — never the words 'students', 'textbook', or 'the chapter'; call the materials 'the source' or by the document's name. (10) VISUALS: use ONLY real figures present in the retrieved excerpts, each on its own slide (0.75+ textwidth, at most two short lines of text); never write a caption for a figure that is not on the slide. (11) When a slide cites a named standard, article, or organization, put its SOURCE URL from the excerpts at the bottom. (12) NEVER invent a named example, number, quote, or citation — if it is not in the excerpts, teach it generically or leave it out. (13) AI appears on at most 2 slides per session, as context only (the framing line: AI is only as good as the data behind it), never as a slide's subject. (14) SCOPE DISCIPLINE: before writing each slide, check it belongs to THIS session's objective and its EXCLUDE list; drop any slide that restates an earlier session or drifts into a later one — a shorter on-objective session beats a longer drifting one.
